paragraphs: Personalizing a system for a new user means learning what they want before there is any interaction history to consult. Asking about every possible preference is impractical, especially when only a few matter to that person. This paper uses correlations across users to make those early questions more informative: a preference for detailed explanations, for example, may provide evidence about a preference for worked examples.

CAPE separates population learning from individual adaptation. Offline, it learns a structured model of how preferences relate, using latent variables to represent underlying patterns. Online, it updates beliefs about a particular user through Bayesian inference, without retraining the model. This decomposition lets information from a small number of answers inform a broader preference estimate.

Across four reasoning domains, CAPE reports 80.8% alignment with ground-truth preferences, compared with 68.5% for end-to-end reinforcement learning. It also needs three to five times fewer interactions and adapts twice as often. Even simple belief models outperform the reinforcement-learning approach, supporting the value of the decomposition itself.
icml-2026-cold-start-personalization-via.tldr: CAPE combines learned preference correlations with online Bayesian questioning to personalize LLM systems with fewer interactions.

paragraphs: A prediction set can include the correct answer at the desired rate overall while behaving differently for particular inputs. Conformal prediction's marginal coverage guarantees address the overall rate, but evaluating these local differences remains difficult. This paper develops diagnostics for conditional coverage by translating the problem into classification.

The central result connects coverage violations to predictive performance: conditional coverage is violated exactly when some classifier can achieve lower risk than the target-coverage reference. The authors call the resulting metrics excess risk of the target coverage, or ERT. With an appropriate loss, the risk improvement conservatively estimates discrepancies measured by L1 or L2 distance. Different choices can distinguish excessive coverage from insufficient coverage and accommodate targets that vary across inputs.

Experiments show that modern classifiers give these diagnostics much greater statistical power than the simple classifiers behind established metrics such as CovGap. The authors also compare conformal methods and release a package containing ERT and earlier metrics. The contribution makes conditional reliability more measurable; it does not turn a coverage diagnostic into a conditional guarantee.
icml-2026-conditional-coverage-diagnosti.tldr: ERT uses classification performance to detect and conservatively quantify local coverage errors in conformal prediction.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a dynamical system involves more than predicting its next observation. The aim is to learn a model that reproduces the system's behavior over long periods and can reveal how it works. Piecewise-linear recurrent networks are useful because their mathematical structure supports analysis, but existing versions advance through discrete time steps. That creates a mismatch with continuously evolving processes and complicates irregularly timed observations.

This paper develops continuous-time piecewise-linear recurrent networks, or cPLRNNs. Their training and simulation algorithm exploits the linear structure within individual regions to bypass numerical integration. The approach seeks to retain the analytical advantages of piecewise-linear models while representing evolution directly in continuous time.

The authors also show how equilibria and limit cycles can be identified semi-analytically in trained models. These objects describe persistent states and repeating behavior, making them useful for understanding the reconstructed dynamics. They compare cPLRNNs with discrete-time counterparts and neural ordinary differential equations on reconstruction benchmarks, including systems with hard-threshold discontinuities. The abstract reports these comparisons without specifying a performance ranking.
icml-2026-continuous-time-piecewise-line.tldr: Continuous-time piecewise-linear recurrent networks exploit their structure for simulation without numerical integration and for mathematical analysis of learned dynamics.

paragraphs: An agent's behavior can change as its tools, updates, or interactions evolve. A representation built from its answers at one moment offers only a snapshot, making it difficult to track changes across a collection of agents. This paper introduces Temporal Data Kernel Perspective Space, or TDKPS, to represent agents jointly across time.

The framework pairs these representations with hypothesis tests for behavioral change. Some tests operate on individual agents, while others examine groups. Because the setting is black-box, the framework monitors behavior without requiring access to agents' internal mechanisms. Jointly representing agents over time provides a basis for comparing their evolving responses rather than treating every time point as a separate analysis.

The authors evaluate the tests in simulations inspired by evolving digital personas, including how their behavior depends on important hyperparameters. In a natural experiment, detected changes correlate sensitively, specifically, and significantly with an external real-world event. This supports the framework's use for monitoring behavioral dynamics, while the reported association does not by itself establish that the event caused every detected shift.
icml-2026-detecting-perspective-shifts-i.tldr: TDKPS represents agents across time and applies statistical tests to detect individual and group behavioral changes.

paragraphs: Continual pre-training adapts a general language model by training it further on specialized material. This paper examines what changes inside model weights during adaptation to mathematics, instructions, code, and natural text. It uses singular value decomposition to separate the strength of weight-matrix components from their directions.

The authors find that component strengths remain largely unchanged, while adaptation mainly changes their directions. Attention heads also differ substantially in how important their updates are, and those differences depend on the domain. Using a head-importance criterion, the authors remove up to 60% of head updates without measurable quality loss. Restoring low-importance heads to their original pre-trained weights can even improve benchmark accuracy by up to 4% over the fully trained model.

A further finding concerns connections between domain-adapted checkpoints. Linear interpolation between them produces smooth changes in domain quality without notable degradation on either domain in the reported analysis. Together, these results show that adaptation is unevenly distributed across heads and that some learned updates can be unnecessary or counterproductive. Diffract provides an open-source toolkit for conducting this spectral analysis at scale.
icml-2026-diffract-spectral-view-of-llm-.tldr: Spectral analysis finds that domain adaptation mainly changes weight directions, with many attention-head updates removable without measurable quality loss.

paragraphs: Deep state space models describe time series through hidden states that produce noisy observations. Learning these models at scale is difficult because training must account for both the unobserved dynamics and the measurements. The paper focuses on the gap between two established approaches to this problem.

One approach uses an auto-encoding model and optimizes a variational lower bound. Another differentiates through sequential Monte Carlo algorithms, which can support both discriminative and generative tasks. The latter approach has a hardware bottleneck: its forward computation is inherently sequential, so later work depends on earlier results. That limits how effectively training can use modern parallel hardware.

The authors introduce parallel variational Monte Carlo, or PVMC, to bridge these approaches and train models for both task types. Across their benchmark experiments, PVMC matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance while training ten times faster than the fastest competing SMC-based method. The result combines predictive or generative quality with a substantial training-speed improvement in the evaluated settings, addressing a central obstacle to scaling hidden-state time-series models.
icml-2026-efficient-learning-of-deep-sta.tldr: PVMC trains deep state space models with competitive or better benchmark performance and tenfold faster training than the fastest tested SMC-based competitor.

paragraphs: Concept erasure aims to stop a text-to-image model from generating an unwanted concept by fine-tuning the model. The central question is whether this removes the concept's underlying connections or only suppresses familiar ways of accessing it. This paper investigates that question using a malicious association introduced before erasure.

The authors call the vulnerability an Erasure Evasion Backdoor. An adversary associates a trigger with the concept that will later be removed, and that association survives subsequent erasure. The paper demonstrates the threat under both black-box and white-box adversary settings. It tests six state-of-the-art erasure methods, including methods designed to search for alternative representations of the unwanted concept.

Reported attack success reaches up to 82% for celebrity-identity unlearning and 94% for object erasure, with explicit-content exposure amplified by up to sixteen times. These are maximum reported effects, not uniform outcomes across all settings. The findings reveal that apparently successful erasure can leave an adversarial route to the target concept. The authors also position this vulnerability as a diagnostic for stress-testing future removal methods.
icml-2026-erased-but-not-forgotten-how-b.tldr: Backdoor associations planted before concept erasure can survive it and expose concepts that tested removal methods were intended to suppress.

paragraphs: Latent flow-matching models can produce similar outputs from the same random seed even after their training data or model capacity is reduced. This paper studies that stability and connects it to the flow-matching objective. The authors then use the observation to develop ways of reducing both training and generation costs.

For training, they show that substantially smaller datasets can preserve performance. Under compute constraints, these models converge faster while maintaining quality, reducing training time and potentially the annotation effort required for conditional models. The paper introduces three scoring criteria for identifying informative samples and evaluates them using standard generative-model metrics.

For inference, the authors divide generation between two models. A lightweight architecture handles the first part of the flow trajectory, and a larger model handles the later part. Stability under architectural shrinkage makes this coarse-to-fine strategy useful in the tested settings. Evaluations across multiple datasets show data savings and more than a twofold inference speedup with comparable outputs, demonstrating practical uses of the observed stability.
icml-2026-exploring-and-exploiting-stabi.tldr: Latent flow-matching stability enables smaller training datasets and a two-model generation strategy that more than doubles inference speed in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The Bistable Memory Recurrent Unit was designed to support very low-power recurrent networks. Its quantized states and hysteresis provide persistent memory in a form suited to analog hardware. However, its performance trails other parallelizable recurrent models on complex sequence tasks. This paper identifies blocked gradients during state updates as a key reason for that gap.

The proposed cumulative update formulation restores gradient flow while retaining persistent memory. It creates skip-connections through time, allowing learning signals to pass through state updates more effectively. This produces the Cumulative Memory Recurrent Unit, or CMRU, along with a relaxed version called alpha-CMRU.

Experiments show substantially more stable convergence and less sensitivity to initialization. At small model sizes, the new units match or outperform Linear Recurrent Units and minimal Gated Recurrent Units across diverse benchmarks, with particular strengths on tasks requiring discrete information to persist over long intervals. CMRU also retains quantized states, persistent memory, and noise-resilient dynamics. These results improve sequence-learning performance while preserving properties important for its intended analog implementation.
icml-2026-improving-the-performance-and-.tldr: Cumulative state updates improve low-power recurrent models' gradient flow, training stability, and long-range memory performance while retaining analog-friendly properties.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether visual systems learn more efficiently when they explain images through a generative model. It contrasts learning and inverting a decoder with learning an encoder that directly maps images to representations. The comparison centers on compositional generalization: handling combinations of familiar components that were not encountered during training.

Under a compositional process for generating data, the authors characterize the structural biases each approach needs. For encoders, the required biases are substantially more complex and generally infeasible to impose explicitly through architecture or regularization. For decoders, they have a simpler form that can be enforced directly. The theoretical result therefore suggests a practical advantage for generative learning under the analyzed structure.

Experiments on synthetic images support this distinction. Non-generative methods often fail to generalize compositionally and need large-scale pretraining to improve, whereas generative methods achieve gains without additional data. The findings support the claim that compositional generalization may be easier through decoder learning and inversion. They do not establish that generation is universally necessary for all forms of data-efficient perception.
icml-2026-is-generation-required-for-dat.tldr: Theory and synthetic-image experiments suggest that generative decoders can achieve compositional generalization with simpler enforceable biases than direct encoders.

paragraphs: When estimating unknown parameters, an experimenter can often choose what measurement or experiment to perform next. A useful choice depends on what previous observations have already revealed. JADAI addresses this coupled problem: selecting informative experiments while updating a Bayesian estimate of the parameters throughout the experimental sequence.

The framework trains three components together: a policy, a history network, and an inference network. Its objective combines incremental reductions in posterior error across the sequence, and does not require density evaluations. Joint amortization moves the learning of both design and inference into this end-to-end training process, tying experiment selection to improvements in the evolving parameter estimate.

The inference component uses diffusion models to approximate posterior distributions at every experimental step. This supports high-dimensional posteriors and distributions with multiple distinct plausible explanations, rather than requiring uncertainty to collapse to a single estimate. JADAI achieves superior or competitive results across adaptive-design benchmarks. Its contribution is a unified training framework that coordinates decisions about what to observe with inference about what those observations mean.
icml-2026-jadai-jointly-amortizing-adapt.tldr: JADAI jointly trains experiment selection and diffusion-based Bayesian inference to improve parameter estimation over adaptive experimental sequences.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces numerical precision to make models cheaper to run. Its evaluation often centers on classification accuracy, but vision-language models also need reliable confidence estimates and the ability to recognize unfamiliar inputs. This paper examines those broader effects through more than 700,000 evaluation runs with varying configurations.

The authors find that quantization can improve accuracy, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and resistance to noise at the same time. Those benefits do not extend to covariate shift or spurious correlations in their findings. This distinction matters because better performance against one kind of disruption does not imply improved reliability under every distribution change.

The proposed explanation is spectral filtering. Quantization dampens high-rank spectral components and makes the model rely more on robust, low-rank features. The authors connect this change to the observed gains in generalization and noise tolerance, going beyond an explanation based only on regularization. The study shows that reduced precision can sometimes contribute to reliability as well as efficiency, while keeping the claim tied to the kinds of reliability that actually improved.
icml-2026-less-precise-can-be-more-relia.tldr: Quantization can improve several vision-language reliability measures through spectral filtering, although the reported benefits exclude covariate shift and spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Conditional diffusion models sometimes generate new combinations of familiar elements, but that ability is inconsistent. This paper studies a concrete example: producing images with more objects than appeared during training. Controlled CLEVR experiments show that some models succeed while others fail, motivating an investigation of what internal structure supports this generalization.

The authors prove an exact equivalence between a particular compositional structure, conditional projective composition, and local conditional scores. Here, locality means that scores have sparse dependencies on image pixels and conditioning information. The theory also extends to compositions represented in feature space, such as combinations of style and content. This gives a precise relationship between a defined form of composition and the model's dependencies.

Successful CLEVR models exhibit local conditional scores, while unsuccessful ones do not. More strongly, an intervention that explicitly enforces locality enables length generalization in a previously failing model. The authors also investigate color-conditioned CLEVR and report preliminary evidence of related structure in SDXL. The intervention supports locality as a mechanism in the controlled setting, while the SDXL finding remains preliminary.
icml-2026-local-mechanisms-of-compositio.tldr: A precise locality condition characterizes a form of diffusion-model composition, and enforcing it enables object-count generalization in a previously failing model.

paragraphs: In a streaming bandit problem, options arrive over time and their rewards are initially unknown. This paper adds an expiration rule: only the most recent W options remain valid. The algorithm sees the stream once and has limited memory, measured by how many options it can retain. Rewards follow unknown sub-Gaussian distributions.

The authors analyze two goals under these constraints. Pure exploration seeks a good available option, while regret minimization concerns the cost of the algorithm's choices. For pure exploration, they prove that identifying the exact best option is hard with sublinear memory. Allowing an approximate best option changes the picture and permits an efficient algorithm.

For regret minimization, the paper develops a regret notion for this setting and establishes sharp trade-offs between memory and regret for single-pass algorithms. Experiments complement the theory by illustrating relationships among sampling, memory, and regret. The sliding window makes recency part of the formal problem: an option can become unusable because it is too old, so retaining information and making effective choices must account for expiration.
icml-2026-online-learning-with-recency-a.tldr: Sliding-window bandit theory identifies when limited-memory learning can find approximately best recent options and quantifies memory–regret trade-offs.

paragraphs: Learning a probability distribution requires enough structure to infer it from finitely many observations. Sample compressibility is one such structural property: a distribution family admits a compact description based on samples. Earlier results connected this property to PAC learnability. This paper asks whether the same structure remains useful when the observations have been corrupted.

The analysis assumes additive noise that is independent of the original samples. Under a set of conditions described as necessary and sufficient in the minimax sense, the authors establish that sample-compressible families remain learnable. This makes the guarantee conditional on the noise setting and those conditions, rather than a claim that any corruption can be overcome.

The paper derives sample-complexity bounds for general sample-compressible classes in arbitrary dimensions, using both L2 and total variation distance to assess error. These bounds characterize how much noisy data is sufficient for the learning problem. The contribution extends the information-theoretic role of compression to perturbed observations; the conjecture that every learnable family admits compression is background motivation, not a result claimed here.
icml-2026-provable-bounds-for-the-learna.tldr: Sample-compressible distribution families remain learnable under independent additive noise when the paper's necessary and sufficient conditions hold.

paragraphs: A long written reasoning trace does not necessarily show when a model settled on its answer. This paper compares three ways of examining that timing: probing internal activations, forcing an early answer, and monitoring the visible chain of thought. The analysis covers DeepSeek-R1 671B and GPT-OSS 120B.

For easy recall-oriented MMLU questions, the eventual answer can be decoded from activations well before a monitor can identify it from the reasoning text. The authors interpret this as evidence of performative reasoning: generation continues after strong internal confidence has developed. Difficult multihop GPQA-Diamond questions show a contrasting pattern of genuine reasoning. Backtracking and apparent breakthroughs occur almost exclusively when probes detect large belief changes, suggesting these visible events often reflect real uncertainty.

The authors use probe signals to stop generation early, reducing token use by up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond while maintaining similar accuracy. The findings support adapting computation to the question and internal state, rather than assuming all visible reasoning tokens contribute equally.
icml-2026-reasoning-theater-disentanglin.tldr: Internal probes reveal that some reasoning continues after answers are already decodable, enabling substantial token savings through early stopping.

paragraphs: Softmax attention is difficult to analyze because of its nonlinear structure. This paper studies a single attention layer by representing input tokens through a probability measure, allowing finite prompts and an infinite-prompt limit to be treated within one framework. For independent, identically distributed centered Gaussian inputs, the limiting softmax operator acts linearly on the input-token measure.

The authors quantify the connection to finite prompts through non-asymptotic concentration bounds on both outputs and gradients. These bounds describe how quickly a finite-prompt model approaches the limiting one. They also prove that concentration remains stable throughout training in general in-context learning settings with sub-Gaussian tokens, making the connection relevant to learning dynamics rather than only a fixed model.

For in-context linear regression, the tractable infinite-prompt dynamics support analysis of training at finite prompt lengths. When prompts are sufficiently long, optimization analyses for linear attention can transfer to softmax attention under the paper's framework. The result provides a route to understanding softmax training through a simpler limiting structure, while retaining explicit input assumptions and prompt-length conditions.
icml-2026-softmax-as-linear-attention-in.tldr: Under stated input assumptions, long-prompt softmax attention approaches a linear limit that makes its outputs, gradients, and training dynamics tractable.

paragraphs: Spectral gradient methods change an update by retaining directional information while discarding scale. This paper investigates why that can help using a nonlinear phase-retrieval model with Gaussian inputs whose variance differs across directions. The model is equivalent to a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation and fixed weights in its second layer.

The main theoretical setting has a dominant variance direction orthogonal to the true signal. During the early escape phase, ordinary gradient descent multiplicatively amplifies high-variance directions even though they contain no useful signal. Under strong anisotropy, this pulls the updates away from alignment with the quantity being learned. Spectral gradient descent removes this magnification effect, giving more stable alignment and faster contraction of noise.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical account and show that the same phenomena persist for more general anisotropic covariance structures. The contribution identifies a concrete mechanism by which spectral updates can help: they prevent irrelevant variance from dominating early learning. This is an explanation established through the analyzed model, rather than a universal performance guarantee for every spectral optimizer or deep network.
icml-2026-spectral-gradient-descent-miti.tldr: In an anisotropic phase-retrieval model, spectral gradient descent avoids amplifying high-variance irrelevant directions and improves alignment with the true signal.

paragraphs: Generating trajectories is challenging when small perturbations can produce different futures and interactions span several spatial and temporal scales. STFlow addresses this problem with a generative model that combines graph neural networks and hierarchical convolutions. The goal is probabilistic trajectory simulation for systems such as interacting bodies, molecules, and moving people.

Its central change concerns the starting distribution used in flow matching. Instead of beginning from Gaussian noise, STFlow uses conditioned random walks through data-dependent couplings. This informed starting point reduces the transport cost involved in turning the initial distribution into the desired trajectory distribution. The authors connect that simpler learning task to more efficient training and inference.

The method is evaluated on N-body systems, molecular dynamics, and human trajectory forecasting. Across those benchmarks, it achieves the lowest prediction errors while using fewer simulation steps and showing improved scalability. The findings support the value of building trajectory structure into the generation starting point: a more suitable prior can reduce the work needed to learn and simulate complex temporal behavior.
icml-2026-stflow-data-coupled-flow-match.tldr: STFlow starts flow matching from conditioned random walks to improve trajectory prediction efficiency, accuracy, and scalability across evaluated systems.

paragraphs: An agent can answer a document question correctly after searching extensively, but accuracy alone does not reveal whether it searched strategically. This paper introduces MADQA to examine that distinction. The benchmark contains 2,250 human-authored questions grounded in 800 varied PDF documents, with its design guided by Classical Test Theory to distinguish different levels of agent ability.

The evaluation protocol measures the trade-off between accuracy and effort. That makes search behavior part of the assessment rather than treating every correct answer as equally effective. The strongest evaluated agents can match human searchers in overall accuracy, yet they tend to succeed on different questions. Their behavior indicates that extensive search compensates for weak strategic planning.

The agents also remain nearly 20% short of oracle performance and persist in unproductive loops. These findings show why matching a human accuracy score can conceal important differences in how answers are found. The released dataset and evaluation harness support comparisons that account for both success and the effort spent achieving it.
icml-2026-strategic-navigation-or-stocha.tldr: MADQA shows that agents can match human document-search accuracy while relying on more brute-force behavior and weaker strategic planning.

paragraphs: Survival data record how long it takes for an event to occur, but observation can end before the event is seen. This right-censoring makes synthetic survival data more complicated than ordinary tables: a generator must reproduce both event timing and the process that leaves some outcomes incomplete. SurvDiff is a diffusion model designed around that joint requirement.

The model generates mixed-type covariates, event times, and right-censoring together. Its survival-specific loss encodes time-to-event structure and directly optimizes for downstream survival tasks. This connects the generation objective to how the resulting records will be used, while targeting realistic event-time distributions and preservation of the censoring mechanism.

Across multiple medical datasets, SurvDiff outperforms state-of-the-art generative baselines on both distributional fidelity and survival-model evaluation metrics. Those two forms of evaluation address complementary goals: resembling the source data and retaining information useful for survival analysis. The authors present it, to their knowledge, as the first end-to-end diffusion model explicitly developed for synthetic survival data, emphasizing the value of incorporating the task's incomplete-observation structure.
icml-2026-survdiff-a-diffusion-model-for.tldr: SurvDiff jointly generates patient covariates, event times, and censoring to improve synthetic survival data fidelity and downstream usefulness.

paragraphs: Theoretical claims about transformer capabilities often depend on attention mechanisms or numerical precision unlike those used in practice. This paper studies standard softmax transformer decoders with rounded activations and attention weights. It allows model depth and width to grow logarithmically with context length, bringing the computational analysis closer to practical architectural choices.

The proof first constructs hardmax transformers with three-valued activations and clearly separated attention scores that simulate Turing machines using chain of thought. Those constructions are then converted into equivalent softmax transformers without requiring the unrealistic parameter sizes or activation precision of earlier approaches. The construction establishes expressive capability under the specified resource scaling.

The authors also analyze summarized chain of thought. In that setting, simulation requires model size growing logarithmically with a space bound rather than a time bound, yielding a more efficient resource dependence. Experiments on Sudoku find that the theory's predictions align better with learnability than earlier high-precision results. This empirical connection complements the expressivity result, which concerns what these models can represent rather than guaranteeing that training will discover every construction.
icml-2026-the-expressive-power-of-low-pr.tldr: Low-precision softmax transformers can simulate Turing machines with chain of thought, with more favorable model-size scaling under summarized reasoning.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must sometimes tolerate workers that behave maliciously or incorrectly. Data poisoning restricts corruption to workers' local training data, while Byzantine failures allow arbitrary corrupted communication. Earlier optimization guarantees can look similar under these two threats. This paper asks whether they also have similar consequences for generalization to unseen data.

The authors analyze algorithmic stability, which connects sensitivity to changes in training data with generalization guarantees. With f misbehaving workers among n workers, they show that data poisoning adds a stability degradation of order f/(n−f) for an algorithm with optimal optimization guarantees. Under Byzantine failures, they establish a lower bound of order sqrt(f/(n−2f)) on the degradation.

These results expose a fundamental separation: arbitrary communication corruption produces strictly worse generalization rates than those achievable when corruption is confined to local data. The tight stability analysis explains why comparable optimization guarantees do not settle the question of performance beyond training. The choice of threat model therefore changes the theoretical reliability guarantees available for robust distributed learning.
icml-2026-tight-stability-bounds-for-rob.tldr: Tight stability bounds show that Byzantine communication failures permit worse generalization guarantees than corruption confined to workers' training data.

paragraphs: Complex forecasting architectures do not automatically outperform shallow linear models on time series. This paper investigates that puzzle through the hypothesis that a useful forecasting model should learn a direct link between past and future data points. The authors call this ability learning dynamics and develop the PRO-DYN nomenclature to analyze how existing models provide it.

Their analysis identifies two patterns. Underperforming architectures learn dynamics only partially, at most, and placing the dynamics block at the end of a model is especially important. This shifts attention from the broad choice of backbone to the specific computation that turns historical information into future predictions, including where that computation occurs.

Systemic and empirical studies support these observations across models with different backbones and varying performance. The authors use the findings to propose a simple plug-and-play methodology for designing or improving forecasting models. The contribution is an architectural perspective grounded in the studied models: examining the direct past-to-future link can help explain performance differences and guide changes without making model complexity itself the organizing principle.
icml-2026-time-series-forecasting-throug.tldr: PRO-DYN links forecasting performance to how models learn past-to-future dynamics and where that computation sits in the architecture.

paragraphs: Variational inference motivates optimization problems in which the objects being adjusted are probability distributions. This paper focuses on Gaussian distributions and introduces a zeroth-order method, meaning it does not rely on objective gradients. Rather than following one deterministic optimization path, the method uses an interacting population of Gaussian particles.

The particles explore stochastically and coordinate through a consensus-based optimization mechanism designed to organize them around global minima. To make the calculations efficient, the authors introduce Linearized Bures–Wasserstein space, a new parametrization of Gaussian measures. This representation supplies the computational setting for the interactions and movement of the Gaussian particles.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the dynamics are well posed and studies convergence through a mean-field approximation. Numerical experiments on variational inference show robustness and better performance than a deterministic gradient-based method for low-dimensional targets that are not log-concave. The reported empirical advantage is specific to that setting. Together, the geometry, population search, and analysis provide an alternative way to optimize Gaussian approximations when a deterministic gradient method is less effective.
icml-2026-variational-inference-via-gaus.tldr: A gradient-free population of interacting Gaussian particles offers an effective variational-inference optimizer for the tested low-dimensional, non-log-concave targets.
